lesson.title: What Really Comes Out of the Flask: Actual Yield
lesson.summary: Actual yield is the mass of product a chemist actually collects and weighs after running a reaction in the lab, and it is almost always somewhat less than the theoretical yield calculated on paper.
lesson.body:
Theoretical yield is a calculation you can do before ever touching a beaker. Actual yield is the opposite: it is a number you can only get by doing the experiment, isolating the product, and putting it on a balance. There is no formula for actual yield. It is raw experimental data, and that is exactly what makes it valuable, because it tells you what really happened rather than what should have happened in an ideal world.

Actual yield is essentially always less than or equal to theoretical yield, and in practice it is almost always strictly less. There are several reasons a real reaction falls short of the theoretical ceiling. The reaction might not go to completion, especially if it is reversible and reaches equilibrium before all the limiting reagent is consumed. Side reactions can divert some of the starting material into unwanted byproducts instead of the desired product. Starting materials are rarely perfectly pure, so some of the mass you weighed out was never able to react at all. And even when the chemistry itself goes perfectly, the physical process of isolating a product, filtering a precipitate, transferring a liquid between containers, or drying a solid, all cause some small amount of material to be lost along the way.

Continuing the zinc chloride example from the previous chapter, imagine a student runs the reaction Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 using 13.0 g of zinc, which calculation showed has a theoretical yield of 27.1 g of ZnCl2. The student filters the resulting solution to remove any unreacted solid, evaporates the water carefully, and dries the solid ZnCl2 to a constant mass. When they weigh the dry product, the balance reads 24.8 g. That 24.8 g is the actual yield. It is smaller than the theoretical 27.1 g, which is expected and normal, but by itself the number 24.8 g does not tell you whether that gap is a big problem or a small, unavoidable one.

To judge whether 24.8 g represents a successful run or a run gone wrong, actual yield has to be measured against theoretical yield directly, as a ratio rather than a standalone number. That comparison is exactly what percent yield provides, and it is the natural next step once both quantities are in hand.
